content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

`cmd/entire/cli/dispatch_wizard_scope.go:99-115`

<result>Read the diff, the huh v2.0.3 source, and the surrounding CLI infrastructure. Six altitude findings.

## Findings

**1. `ensureScope` in `WithHideFunc` — the form is being used as a scheduler, and huh's model doesn't support it**
`/Users/alisha/.marvin/worktrees/cli/cli-dispatch-jurisdiction/cmd/entire/cli/dispatch_wizard.go:282-291, 317-321, 339-345`
Hide funcs are not "the form goroutine" in the benign sense the comment assumes. `Form.isGroupHidden` is called from `UpdateFieldPositions`, which runs (a) synchronously inside `huh.NewForm` (`form.go:127`, reached via `uiform.New`) and (b) on **every `tea.KeyPressMsg` inside `Form.Update`** (`form.go:628`), plus at `form.go:519/592/611`. So the blocking `loadScope()` join lands on the bubbletea event loop the first keypress after the user picks Cloud: up to `dispatchWizardScopeTimeout` (10s) plus an unbounded gateway repo-list call with the UI frozen, no spinner, and no Ctrl-C. The background `go loadScope()` only helps if the user dawdles on Mode — the "rarely waits" premise isn't guaranteed by anything. Secondarily, the comment's own safety argument doesn't hold: `state.jurisdiction`/`state.scope` are written here (event loop) and read by `loadRepos` from a `tea.Cmd` goroutine (`field_multiselect.go:338`) with no synchronization.
*Deeper fix:* let huh own the async. Drop `ensureScope` entirely and put the wait inside the jurisdiction `OptionsFunc` — that already runs on a `tea.Cmd` goroutine under huh's own loading spinner (`field_select.go:364-372`) — returning options in default-first order so `Select` seeds `state.jurisdiction` from option[0] via huh's normal binding instead of a manual write. `hasPicker` then becomes a read of a value cached by that same `sync.OnceValue`, so the hide func stays a pure predicate. The alternative — resolve the scope before `NewAccessibleForm` behind the spinner in `dispatch_tui.go` — is simpler but makes Local-mode users pay for cloud calls.
*Cost:* ~40 lines in `runDispatchWizard`, one new test driving the form; roughly half a day. Requires accepting that the jurisdiction default is expressed as option ordering rather than an assignment.

**2. Fourth hand-rolled "read the whole repo index" call site**
`dispatch_wizard_scope.go:141-166` (and the constant at `:15-18`)
`newCellCoreClient()` + `ListRepos(ctx, ListReposParams{})` + a 10s timeout + an `index.Truncated` warning is already written out at `search_cmd.go:525-543`, in `search_v4.go`'s `listFullIndex`, and in `repo_mirror.go:866/910`. The comment even says the timeout is "the same budget code search gives the same call" — the constant was copied rather than shared.
*Deeper fix:* one `listRepoIndex(ctx)` helper beside `cell_fanout.go`, which already owns the index→routing vocabulary, owning client construction, the timeout constant, and the truncation warning; the wizard keeps only the entries→jurisdictions mapping.
*Cost:* ~20 lines moved, but it touches both search paths, so their tests must be re-run. Small.

**3. "repo → ready jurisdictions" is now built two different ways**
`dispatch_wizard_scope.go:141-166` vs `dispatch_jurisdiction.go:66-88`
Reusing `readyPlacementJurisdictions` is the right call and I'd keep it. But the map around it is now duplicated: the hint builds it per-repo via `lookupRepoIndexEntry` on a 3s-per-repo budget keyed by the user's typed slug; the wizard builds it from one full index read on 10s keyed by lowercased slug. Two shapes, two budgets, two key conventions for the same question.
*Deeper fix:* one `repoReadyJurisdictions(ctx, client, repos ...string)` in `dispatch_jurisdiction.go` (empty variadic = full index), returning a lowercase-keyed map; both callers use it.
*Cost:* ~40 lines consolidated. The real work is reconciling the two timeout policies (garnish-on-an-error vs blocking-a-picker) — they may legitimately differ, in which case pass the budget in.

**4. `auth.HomeJurisdiction` is at the right layer but claims authority it doesn't have**
`/Users/alisha/.marvin/worktrees/cli/cli-dispatch-jurisdiction/cmd/entire/cli/auth/cell_data_api.go:578-592`
The layer is defensible: `resolveJurisdiction` (`:381-397`) routes on the `home_jurisdiction` claim, so for "where would we route by default" the claim *is* the operative value, and `resolveCellSubject` is unexported so the wizard can't compose this itself. The altitude problem is the name and doc: `auth.go:441-448` establishes that `/me`'s `global.homeJurisdiction` is *authoritative* for the home jurisdiction with the claim as fallback. There are now two exported-ish answers to "what is my home jurisdiction" that can silently disagree (stale claim after a home migration) with nothing linking them.
*Deeper fix:* name it for what it is — `RoutingHomeJurisdiction`, or `HomeJurisdictionFromActiveLogin` — and say in the doc that the profile answer is `/me`'s. Or, more thoroughly, have `auth` expose the single `/me`-preferred resolver and let `runAuthStatus` call it, keeping the claim-only path as the explicitly-named routing variant.
*Cost:* rename is trivial (one call site). Unifying is medium and drags a `/me` round-trip into a path that deliberately avoids one.

**5. `showRepoPicker()` is now production-dead**
`dispatch_wizard.go:132-134`
The repo group's hide func was rewritten to `state.isLocal()` inline (to hang the `ensureScope()` side effect off it), leaving `showRepoPicker` referenced only by `dispatch_wizard_test.go:121/126`. The state predicate that used to express "which groups show" was bypassed rather than extended.
*Deeper fix:* delete it and its two test assertions (it falls out naturally once finding 1 restores pure predicates).
*Cost:* trivial.

**6. `resolveCloudRepos` is a third enforcement point for "one dispatch, one jurisdiction"**
`dispatch_wizard.go:107-130`
The invariant is now enforced in three places: the restricted option list, huh's own narrowing (`updateOptionsMsg` → `selectOptions` → `updateValue` rewrites `state.selectedRepos` to the intersection with the new option set, `field_multiselect.go:362-370`), and this filter. None of them is `dispatch/options.go`, which owns `Options` and whose consumer — the cell — is what actually 404s on a cross-jurisdiction repo. A wizard state accessor silently discarding a user's selection is the wrong home for a domain rule (mitigated: the confirm summary shows the surviving list).
*Deeper fix:* if the rule is real, validate it in `resolveDispatchOptions` so `--repos` + `--jurisdiction` gets the same treatment as the wizard; the wizard's filter then becomes redundant with huh's narrowing and can go.
*Cost:* low-medium — needs a decision on whether the flag path should hard-error instead of silently dropping (I'd expect error there, drop here).

## Explicit non-findings

- **Two catalogues is not avoidable.** `api.Repository` (`api/repositories.go:11-14`) carries only `full_name` + `checkpoint_count`; `coreapi.RepoIndexEntry` carries `Placements` but no checkpoint count. No single source answers "offerable and placed where". Only the join's *location* is debatable, and findings 2-3 cover that.
- **"READY placements only" is right and consistent.** It reuses `readyPlacementJurisdictions`, so the wizard offers exactly the slugs the placement hint offers and the `--jurisdiction` flag accepts. Its divergence from `routedRepoPlacement` (one elected processing primary, ready) is correct, not an inconsistency: that rule exists to dedup mirrors for *search indexing*, whereas the hint's existence proves a cell answers dispatch for any ready placement. Worth a one-line comment in `dispatch_wizard_scope.go` pointing at `routedRepoPlacement` to say the difference is deliberate.
- **`insecureHTTP: false` hardcoded** in `defaultResolveDispatchWizardHome` matches the wizard's existing stance (`state.resolve()` already passes `false` for `InsecureHTTPAuth`), so it's pre-existing, not introduced here.</result>

content.text:
`/simplify` done — committed as `4d7f702ac` (five commits on the branch, nothing pushed).

## What was fixed

**The big one (efficiency + altitude agreed):** the picker loaded its catalogue from a group hide func. huh evaluates those on the Bubble Tea event loop on every keypress, so the first step into cloud mode froze the form — no spinner, no Ctrl-C — until three network calls returned; the default it wrote into form state also raced with the repo picker's options goroutine; and the eager background load ran for local-mode users who never need it. Now the Jurisdiction select's `OptionsFunc` does the loading (huh runs it off the event loop under its own spinner, only in cloud mode) and the default is expressed as option order, which huh binds into the state itself. Hide funcs are pure predicates again.

**Smaller:**
- Scope is precomputed once (jurisdiction → repos map, sorted keys, default) instead of five overlapping catalogue scans per render; `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(...))` replaces the hand-rolled set→sort.
- Dropped the redundant selection filter and `state.scope` — huh already narrows the bound selection when options change (two reviewers verified against huh's source).
- `showRepoPicker` is live again instead of inlined; `loadRepos` misnomer gone.
- `auth.HomeJurisdiction` → `HomeJurisdictionFromActiveLogin`, documented as the routing claim, not the authoritative `/me` home.
- Tests collapsed into one table; unused stub parameter removed. Net −46 lines.

**Skipped (noted):**
- A shared `listRepoIndex` helper for the four call sites that read the whole control-plane index (search ×2, mirror, wizard) — worthwhile, but touches the search paths; separate change.
- Merging the hint's per-repo lookup with the wizard's full-index map — different budgets/keying are deliberate.
- Deriving home from the token the placements client already minted (saves one refresh) — the client interface doesn't expose it; small win, not worth widening the seam now.

Verification: lint 0 issues; 10,035 unit tests pass; wizard tests green under `-race`.

Every `NewRefreshingLoginProvider` constructs a fresh `tokenmanager.Manager` (`auth/refresh.go:124`), and `Manager.Refresh` reads the store on *every* call, even the fast path (`tokenmanager.go:945-958` `ensureFreshLogin` → `loadTokenSet`), where `contextTokenStore.LoadTokens` does two `tokenstore.Get` keyring calls (`auth/refresh.go:41,55`). `contexts.Load` has no memoization either (`contexts.go:73-83`, file-locked read each time). Only the *exchanged* token cache is in-process, and it is per-Manager (`m.cache`), so it never helps here.

**Expired-JWT contention is serialized but harmless.** The three Managers share one cross-process lock path (`processLock()` keyed on ClientID+Issuer, `tokenmanager.go:765-767`), and `freshOrProceed` re-reads the store after each gate (`:996-1005`), so late waiters reuse the first grant rather than burning three rotations. Redundant, not incorrect.

**Simpler path exists.** Goroutine 3 adds nothing goroutine 2 doesn't already hold: `auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget()` returns `TokenSource` yielding the bare login JWT (`control_plane.go:33-35,102`), and `auth.HomeJurisdictionFromLoginJWT` (`cell_data_api.go:600`) reads the claim from it, so the placements goroutine could derive `home` from the same token (mind the `ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypass, which `coreapi.New` and `resolveCellSubject` both honour but `ResolveControlPlaneTarget` does not — the merged path must keep that parity). Note the `coreapi.Client` itself exposes no token accessor (only `CoreOrigin`, `client.go:135`), so the fix is at the target level, not the client.

**Nuance:** goroutine 1 predates this PR (`dispatch_wizard.go:26` exists at HEAD; diff line 1438 shows the old call), so the PR adds two new resolutions, not three; and because all three run concurrently, wall-clock cost is roughly the slowest keyring read, not the sum. Code review done and fixes committed (`bab2c5526`). Six commits on the branch, nothing pushed.

## Review findings and what I did

**Fixed**
- **Accessible-mode crash (real bug):** huh's accessible runner ignores hide funcs and never evaluates `OptionsFunc`, so the new Jurisdiction select had zero options and panicked on Enter — even in local mode. In `ACCESSIBLE=1` the wizard now skips the picker (`--jurisdiction` still works) and resolves the repo list up front, which also unbreaks the pre-existing dynamic repo list there.
- **Unverified selector:** the response's `jurisdiction` stamp is decoded again and checked against what was sent. A *different* stamp fails (wrong-region result); a *missing* stamp (older gateway) is tolerated with a warning — I chose warn over fail so the flag doesn't hard-error against today's production gateway during rollout.
- **Hint re-offering the failed jurisdiction:** the placement hint now excludes the jurisdiction that 404'd (the selector sent, or home when none was).
- **Unselectable repos:** with home unknown, unplaced repos now stay selectable under a plain "Home" choice instead of falling into no bucket. This also surfaced a real edge in the default pick that the new table case caught.
- **Single-page index read:** the control-plane index is now walked across pages (bounded at 5000 entries) via the existing `fetchPagesBounded`.
- **Options-goroutine race:** the repo picker reads the jurisdiction through an atomic snapshot kept by the select's accessor, not the shared field huh writes on the event loop.
- Own sentence for the repo-not-found error instead of probing gateway prose; dead branch in `doJSON` removed; validation error names the slug once.

**Skipped (noted)**
- Deriving home from the token the control-plane client already minted (saves one refresh): the suggested path may not honour `ENTIRE_TOKEN`; small win, left as is.
- Routing `entire api --jurisdiction` through the shared normaliser: outside this change's surface.

Verification: lint 0 issues; 10,037 unit tests pass; dispatch and wizard tests green under `-race`.

# Getting a PR Ready for Review

The goal is a branch that a reviewer can look at with confidence: caught up with
the base branch, no conflicts, no regressions, a PR open (ready for review), and
CI green. This skill is the step *before* requesting review — it does not merge
the PR and does not post it anywhere.

Work through the phases below in order, but **scope to what's needed**. If the
branch is already merged-clean and only CI is red, skip straight to the CI
phase. If there's no remote branch yet, you'll still do everything. Tell the
user which phases you're running and why.

## Guiding principles

These matter more than the mechanics — internalize them, because the mechanics
serve them:

- **Never mask a problem to make a check pass.** Deleting a failing test,
  loosening an assertion, adding `// eslint-disable` over a real lint error,
  `--no-verify`, or `continue-on-error` turns a red check green while leaving the
  bug in place. That defeats the entire point of getting review-ready. Fix the
  underlying cause. If a check is failing for a reason genuinely unrelated to
  this branch (flaky test, pre-existing breakage on main), say so explicitly and
  ask the user rather than papering over it.
- **Conflict resolution preserves both intents.** A merge conflict means two
  changes touched the same place. Resolving it is not "pick a side" — it's
  understanding what *each* side was trying to do and producing code that honors
  both. Blindly taking `--ours` or `--theirs` is how regressions sneak in.
- **Verify before you push, then verify again in CI.** Local verification is
  fast and catches most regressions before they cost a CI cycle. CI is the
  source of truth. Both matter.
- **Review your own diff before you ship it.** Build/test/lint prove the code
  *runs*; they don't prove the *change* is clean. Read the full branch diff with
  fresh eyes for two things a green build hides: regressions the change slipped in
  (behavior quietly altered, a caller left on an old contract, a dropped edge
  case) and dead or unused code it created (functions/params/imports/types nothing
  references, unreachable branches, leftover debug or commented-out code,
  scaffolding wired to nothing). Ship the change, not the scaffolding around it.
- **Stop and ask when the right answer is ambiguous**, especially on conflict
  resolution where the two sides represent real product decisions. A wrong guess
  here is worse than a question.

## Phase 1 — Orient

Establish the ground truth before changing anything. Run these read-only:

- `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` — the current branch. If it's `main`/`master`,
  stop: there's nothing to ready-for-review. Ask the user which branch they mean.
- `git status` — confirm a clean working tree. If there are uncommitted changes,
  surface them and ask whether to commit, stash, or abort. Don't merge on top of
  a dirty tree — it tangles your changes with the merge.
- Determine the **base branch**. It's usually `main`, sometimes `master` or a
  release branch. Check `git remote show origin | grep "HEAD branch"` or look at
  what the existing PR targets (Phase 4). Don't assume `main`.
- `gh pr view --json number,state,isDraft,baseRefName,url 2>/dev/null` — does a
  PR already exist for this branch, and what does it target? Remember the answer
  for Phase 4.

Report a one-line plan: which base, whether a PR exists, and which phases you'll
run.

## Phase 2 — Sync the base branch

Get the latest base so the merge reflects reality:

```
git fetch origin <base>
```

Fetching is enough — you merge `origin/<base>` directly in the next phase, so you
don't need to check out and fast-forward your local base branch. (If the user
specifically wants their local base updated too, `git checkout <base> && git pull
--ff-only && git checkout -` does it without surprises.)

## Phase 3 — Merge the base in and resolve conflicts

The user asked for a **merge**, not a rebase — keep it a merge so history and any
in-flight review threads stay intact:

```
git merge origin/<base>
```

**If it merges cleanly**, go to Phase 4 after a quick local verification.

**If there are conflicts**, resolve them deliberately:

1. `git status` and `git diff` to see every conflicted file. Work through them one
   at a time — don't bulk-resolve.
2. For each conflict, understand *both* sides before writing the resolution:
   - `git log --merge -p <file>` shows the commits from each side touching the
     conflict region — this is the fastest way to see intent.
   - If the repo is Entire-enabled and the intent is still unclear, the
     `what-happened` / `explain` skills can recover the reasoning behind a block.
   - Read enough surrounding code to know what each change was accomplishing.
3. Write a resolution that keeps both intents. If side A renamed a function and
   side B added a new caller of the old name, the resolution updates the caller —
   it doesn't drop either change. If the two intents genuinely conflict (both
   changed the same value to different things), that's a product decision: stop
   and ask the user.
4. `git add` each resolved file as you finish it.
5. When all conflicts are resolved, **verify before committing the merge** (next
   phase). Don't `git commit` the merge until the code at least builds — a merge
   commit that doesn't compile is a regression you're about to push.

## Phase 4 — Verify locally & self-review the diff

A merge can produce code that compiles on each side but breaks when combined
("semantic conflicts" git can't detect). Catch these now, cheaply.

Run the project's real verification — discover it rather than guessing. Look for
the commands the repo actually uses (a project skill for running the app/tests,
`Makefile`/`justfile` targets, `package.json` scripts, `go test ./...`, CI config
under `.github/workflows`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`). Run, in roughly this order, what
exists: build → unit tests → lint/typecheck.

> **cli repo — do NOT run the e2e suite locally (temporary, 2026-07-20).** The
> e2e suite (`mise run test:e2e*`, and `test:ci`/`check` which call it) deletes
> the developer's real `~/.claude/projects` transcripts via an unmerged HOME-
> isolation bug. The tasks are locally gated to SKIP (exit 0) — that skip is
> intentional; do not "fix" it or set `ENTIRE_ALLOW_LOCAL_E2E=1`. Verify with
> `mise run test` (unit) + `mise run lint` only; CI runs e2e on isolated runners.

- If verification passes, commit the merge (`git commit` with no `-m` accepts the
  default merge message, or write a short one) and continue.
- If it fails, fix the cause — a semantic conflict you missed, an import that
  moved, a renamed symbol. Re-run until clean, then commit the merge.

Skipping this phase just moves the failure to CI, where it's slower to diagnose.
It's worth doing even when the merge was conflict-free.

### Self-review the branch diff — regressions & dead code

Verification proves the code *runs*; it doesn't prove the *change* is clean. Before
pushing, read the branch's full diff against the base with fresh eyes — this is a
review of the code *this branch introduces*, separate from the build/test pass
above:

```
git diff origin/<base>...HEAD
```

Look for two classes of problem a green build won't reliably flag:

- **Regressions the change introduced** — behavior that changed when it shouldn't
  have; a renamed or re-signatured function with a caller left on the old contract;
  an error path, guard, or edge case dropped in an edit or a conflict resolution; a
  default or constant that silently shifted. Trace each non-trivial hunk to the
  callers it affects and confirm they still hold.
- **Dead / unused code the change created** — new functions, methods, variables,
  parameters, struct fields, types, imports, or constants that nothing references;
  branches that can no longer be reached; a helper added but never wired in; a
  feature-flag path with no live caller; leftover debug logging, commented-out
  code, or TODO stubs. Review naturally sees the *addition* and rarely notices the
  thing is never *used*.

Lean on tooling to find the unused set, then confirm by hand — don't trust it
alone:

- Compiler/linter unused checks (discover what the repo uses): Go flags unused
  locals/imports at build and surfaces unused functions via `go vet` /
  `staticcheck` / `golangci-lint` (and `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode` for
  whole-program dead functions); TypeScript via `tsc --noUnusedLocals
  --noUnusedParameters` and eslint `no-unused-vars`.
- For each new exported symbol the diff adds, grep the repo for references — zero
  hits outside its own definition and test means it's dead.
- If a `dead-code-finder` skill is available, point it at the branch's changes.

Resolve what you find: **remove** dead code this branch introduced (if it's
deliberate scaffolding for an imminent follow-up, say so explicitly and keep it
only with the user's nod); **fix** any regression at its root, never by loosening a
test. If deleting suspected-dead code is risky — it may be reached via reflection,
build tags, code generation, or an external consumer — confirm before removing it
rather than guessing. Keep the scope to *this branch's* diff; don't go hunting
pre-existing dead code across the repo — that's not what getting this PR ready is
about.

## Phase 5 — Push

**Before you push, strip scratch working docs from the branch.** Agents routinely
leave planning/findings scratch files in the worktree — `FINDINGS.md`, `PLAN.md`,
`plan.md`, `*-seed.md`, `DAY_DRIVER_TASK.md`, `NOTES.md`, `TODO.md`, design/
investigation write-ups — that are working artifacts, **not** part of the change.
They must never ship in the PR. Catch them here, before the branch goes remote.

1. List `.md` files this branch adds vs the base, plus any untracked ones in the
   worktree:
   ```
   git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A origin/<base>...HEAD -- '*.md'
   git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all -- '*.md'
   ```
2. Decide each candidate by **intent, not just extension**:
   - **Remove** agent-generated scratch — findings / plan / seed / task-handoff /
     notes docs (typically at the repo root or a scratch dir) created by this
     branch and unrelated to the change under review.
   - **Keep** genuine documentation — anything under `docs/`, `README*`,
     `CHANGELOG*`, ADRs, `CONTRIBUTING*`, or a `.md` the change *legitimately*
     adds (e.g. docs for the feature you just built). When you're unsure whether a
     doc is intended, ask rather than delete.
3. Remove the scratch docs so they can't reach the PR — but **don't destroy work
   you can't recover**: if a findings/investigation write-up looks worth keeping,
   copy it to a durable scratch location (`~/.claude/tmp/…`) first, then delete.
   - Untracked (never committed): delete from disk (`rm <file>`).
   - Already committed on this branch: `git rm <file>` and commit the removal
     (`git commit -m "chore: drop scratch planning/findings docs"`).

Then push:

```
git push -u origin HEAD
```

**Never force-push** — not `--force`, not `--force-with-lease`, not under any
circumstance. If a plain push is rejected because the remote branch has diverged,
that divergence is real work (someone — a person or another agent — pushed to
this branch), and overwriting it loses commits. Instead: fetch, inspect what's
there (`git log HEAD..origin/HEAD --oneline`), and integrate it by merging
`origin/HEAD` into your branch, resolving any conflicts exactly as in Phase 3.
Then push normally. If you can't reconcile it cleanly, stop and hand it to the
user — pushing over their work is never the answer.

## Phase 6 — Open a PR (ready for review) if none exists

If Phase 1 found no PR, create one **ready for review** (not a draft):

```
gh pr create --base <base> --fill
```

`--fill` seeds the title/body from commits; improve the body if it's thin — a
reviewer should be able to tell what changed and why without reading the diff.
Capture the PR URL to report at the end.

**Write the body short and plain.** A PR/trail body is read by a busy human, not
a compiler — optimize for *fast understanding*, not completeness. Aim for a
screenful or less. Follow this shape:

- **What was broken** — the user-visible symptom, in one or two sentences, with a
  concrete example if there is one.
- **Why** — the root cause in plain language. Name mechanisms in words, not
  symbols; skip file paths, line numbers, function names, and constant names (the
  diff has those).
- **The fix** — what you changed, at a conceptual level. A short numbered list is
  fine.
- **Verified** — one line: what you ran (tests/lint) and any key behavioral proof.

Rules: no walls of text, no deep-dive rationale, no citing `identifiersLikeThis`
or `path/to/file.go:123` in the body, no restating the same point three ways.
Keep the interesting-but-non-essential caveats out — if a reviewer needs them,
they'll ask or read the diff. Write like you're explaining it to a teammate in
Slack. If the drafted body is long or hard to follow, cut it down before opening
the PR — the same body goes on the Entire trail, so length there hurts too.

**Keep the trail out of the PR body.** Do not put an `entire-trail-link` comment
block (or any trail link) in the GitHub PR body — the trail is populated *from*
the PR body in the next step, not linked to from the PR. If `--fill` or an
existing body carried a trail-link block over, strip it before settling the body.

If a PR already exists and is still a draft, mark it ready:

```
gh pr ready <number>
```

### Copy the PR body to the Entire trail

Once the PR body is settled (whether you just created the PR or one already
existed), copy that same body onto the branch's Entire trail so the trail and the
PR tell the same story — the GitHub PR body is the source of truth:

1. Read the PR's current body:
   ```
   gh pr view <number> --json body --jq .body
   ```
2. Push it to the trail with the `entire` CLI (defaults to the current branch):
   ```
   entire trail update --body "$PR_BODY"
   ```
   For a PR on a different branch, target it explicitly: `entire trail update
   --branch <headRefName> --body "$PR_BODY"`.

If `entire trail update` reports no trail for the branch, note it and move on —
don't create one just to sync a body unless the user asks. If the `entire` CLI
isn't installed or the repo isn't Entire-enabled, skip this step silently.

## Phase 7 — Make CI green

CI is the gate. Watch it, and fix what fails.

1. Wait for checks to run and report status:
   ```
   gh pr checks --watch
   ```
   (Plain `gh pr checks` for a one-shot snapshot.)
2. **For each failed check**, get the actual failure — don't guess from the
   check's name. Write the failing logs to a local file so you can read and
   re-read them while iterating (this is the standing rule: debug from saved logs,
   don't ask the user to paste them):
   ```
   gh run view <run-id> --log-failed > /tmp/pr-ready-ci-<run-id>.log
   ```
   Then read that file and find the real failure (often buried above the final
   error). For richer context, `gh run view <run-id>` lists the jobs and steps.
3. Diagnose and fix the **root cause** in the code, honoring the "never mask"
   principle above. A failing test means the code is wrong or the test needs a
   legitimate update because behavior intentionally changed — distinguish the two
   honestly. Reproduce locally first when you can; a fix you've confirmed locally
   is far more likely to turn the check green than a blind push.
4. Commit the fix with a clear message, push, and return to step 1. Loop until
   all checks pass.
5. **Know when to stop.** If a check fails for a reason outside this branch's
   control (infra flake, a secret the fork can't access, a failure already
   present on the base branch), don't thrash. State what's failing, why you
   believe it's unrelated, and hand it to the user.

## Phase 8 — Bugbot review

With CI green, get an automated review pass from bugbot before handing off. Run
this *after* CI is green so bugbot reviews the final state of the branch.

1. **Trigger bugbot** by commenting on the PR:
   ```
   gh pr comment <pr-number> --body "bugbot run"
   ```
   Tell the user bugbot has been triggered and you're waiting for its review.
2. **Wait for the review.** Bugbot typically takes ~5 minutes. Record the current
   timestamp (ISO 8601) first, then get the repo slug:
   ```
   gh repo view --json owner,name --jq '"\(.owner.login)/\(.name)"'
   ```
   Poll every 180 seconds (`sleep 180` between checks) for new posts from bugbot.
   Its login is `cursor[bot]` (older setups may show plain `cursor`) — match BOTH,
   and check BOTH post types (line comments AND reviews; a "no issues" verdict
   arrives only as a review body, so polling comments alone misses it):
   ```
   gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr-number}/comments --jq '[.[] | select(.created_at > "TIMESTAMP") | select(.user.login == "cursor[bot]" or .user.login == "cursor") | {id, body, path, line: .original_line, diff_hunk}]'
   gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr-number}/reviews --jq '[.[] | select(.submitted_at > "TIMESTAMP") | select(.user.login == "cursor[bot]" or .user.login == "cursor") | {id, state, body}]'
   ```
   For a review with line comments, fetch them with
   `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr-number}/reviews/{review-id}/comments`.
   If nothing appears after ~10 minutes, tell the user bugbot hasn't responded and
   ask how to proceed rather than waiting indefinitely.
3. **Triage and fix each comment** the same way the rest of this skill works — fix
   the **root cause**, never mask it:
   - Real bugs, security issues, correctness problems → fix them.
   - Reasonable clarity/style improvements → fix them.
   - False positives or suggestions that would make the code worse → skip them,
     and note why.
   Keep fixes minimal and focused on what bugbot flagged; don't refactor
   surrounding code or touch files bugbot didn't comment on. If a bugbot comment
   is ambiguous or represents a product decision, stop and ask the user.
4. **If you made fixes**, verify locally (Phase 4), commit with a clear message,
   push (Phase 5), and **return to Phase 7** — the fixes must pass CI too. Then
   you may re-trigger bugbot if the changes were substantial. If every comment was
   a false positive, say so and move on without committing.

If the repo doesn't use bugbot (commenting does nothing and no review ever
arrives), don't block on it — note that bugbot isn't configured and finish.

## Phase 9 — Address reviews on the Entire trail

Reviewers (people and agents) leave review feedback on the branch's Entire trail
as **findings**. Clear the open ones before handing off, the same root-cause way
as the bugbot phase.

1. **List open findings** for the branch's trail (defaults to the current branch,
   `--status open`, current code version):
   ```
   entire trail finding list --json
   ```
   If the `entire` CLI isn't installed, the repo isn't Entire-enabled, or there's
   no trail, skip this phase silently. If there are no open findings, note that
   and move on. Use `entire trail finding show <finding-id>` for the full detail
   of any finding.
2. **Triage and fix each finding** — fix the **root cause**, never mask it:
   - Real bugs, security, correctness → fix them.
   - Reasonable clarity/style improvements → fix them.
   - False positives or suggestions that would make the code worse → dismiss with
     a reason: `entire trail finding dismiss <finding-id> -m "why"`.
   When a finding carries a unified-diff suggestion that's correct, apply it
   directly (add `--resolve` to close it once the patch lands):
   ```
   entire trail finding apply <finding-id> --resolve
   ```
   (`--check` first if you want to confirm the patch applies cleanly.) When you
   fix a finding by hand instead, mark it resolved with a note:
   ```
   entire trail finding resolve <finding-id> -m "what you changed"
   ```
   If a finding is ambiguous or represents a product decision, stop and ask the
   user rather than guessing.
3. **If you made code fixes**, verify locally (Phase 4), commit with a clear
   message, push (Phase 5), and **return to Phase 7** — the fixes must pass CI
   too. Because the fixes changed the branch, re-copy the PR body to the trail
   (Phase 6) if the body changed. If every finding was a false positive, dismiss
   them with reasons and move on without committing.

## Done

Report concisely:

- Base merged in (and whether there were conflicts, and how you resolved any
  non-obvious ones).
- Local verification result.
- Diff self-review: any regressions caught and fixed, and any dead/unused code the
  branch introduced that you removed (name it) — or that the diff was clean.
- Any scratch planning/findings docs stripped before push (name each, and where
  you stashed a copy if one was worth keeping) — or that there were none.
- PR URL (and whether you created it or it already existed) — note it's **ready
  for review** (not a draft).
- Whether the Entire trail body was copied from the PR body (or why it was skipped).
- Final CI status: all green, or the specific checks still failing and why.
- Bugbot result: how many comments it raised, how many you fixed (and what), how
  many you skipped (and why) — or that bugbot isn't configured for the repo.
- Trail findings: how many open findings were on the trail, how many you resolved
  (and what), how many you dismissed (and why) — or that there was no trail / the
  repo isn't Entire-enabled.

If everything's green and the user wants to request review, point them at the
`post-pr-review` skill — that assigns the PR and posts it to Slack. This skill
deliberately stops short of that.
Running `/pr-ready`. Phase 1 — orienting.

## What was broken

`entire dispatch` always generated from the caller's home region, so a repo placed only elsewhere (e.g. a US-only repo from an AU home) failed with a bare "repository not found". The web app fixed this in entirehq/entire.io#3946 by scoping a dispatch to one jurisdiction; the CLI had no way to say which.

## Why

A dispatch is generated by one regional cell, and each cell only knows repos placed in its own region. The gateway routes a dispatch request by a `?jurisdiction=` selector; without it, home. The CLI never sent one.

## The fix

1. `entire dispatch --jurisdiction <slug>` (`-j`): cloud-only, sent as the gateway's query selector on the existing one-shot generate route (the body is unchanged; nothing is persisted). Omitted means home, so existing behaviour is the default. The gateway's echoed jurisdiction is checked: a different one fails; none (an older gateway) warns.
2. The wizard asks for a jurisdiction before the repo picker, derived from each repo's ready placements in the control-plane index, and only offers repos placed there — a mixed selection can't be expressed. Defaults to home when you have repos there. In accessible mode the picker is skipped (use the flag).
3. A cross-jurisdiction 404 becomes legible: "In AU: repository not found: X. Pick a jurisdiction the repository is mirrored into (`--jurisdiction <slug>`), or mirror it there." plus a best-effort hint of where the repo *is* placed.

Note: the selector only takes effect once the matching gateway change to the generate route ships; until then it is forwarded and ignored (home, as today).

## Verified

`mise run lint` clean; `mise run test` 10,037 tests pass; dispatch/wizard tests green under `-race`. Not driven by hand against a multi-region account.

Manual testing done. Summary of what I actually ran against the built binary:

**Offline / flag path**
- `--help` shows the new flag and examples; wording fixed ("generates", not "stores") and pushed as `b0bb1914f` (CI green again except the approvals gate).
- `--local --jurisdiction us` → rejected; `--jurisdiction 'us east'` → "invalid --jurisdiction … not a valid label".

**Live gateway**
- `--repos entireio/cli --jurisdiction US --since 1d` hit production and got a **502 "Failed to read dispatch data from a repository's region"** from the legacy route. Retrying both `main`'s binary and mine for comparison hit a **429 rate limit**, so I can't yet say whether the 502 is pre-existing; a background retry runs after the window resets and I'll report it. The selector itself can't cause it (today's gateway ignores the query), so I expect it's unrelated. Side observation: the new build prints the parsed message (`"Rate limit exceeded"`) where main prints raw JSON.

**Wizard (driven through a pty with real account data)**
- Cloud → Jurisdiction select loads under a spinner and shows `US (home)`, `AU`, `EU`, `IN`, home first.
- Picking AU lists the AU-mirrored repos (cli, atlas, browser-extension, company-knowledge, entire-api, entire-brain, entire-search, entire.io); US lists a different, larger set.
- Select a US-only repo → Shift+Tab → switch to AU: the stale selection is dropped, as designed. A repo present in both stays selected.

message.content: how can I test it

content.text:
Build the branch binary and run it from any Entire-enabled repo:

```bash
cd ~/.marvin/worktrees/cli/cli-dispatch-jurisdiction
go build -o /tmp/entire-dev ./cmd/entire
```

**1. Wizard (the main thing to eyeball)**
```bash
/tmp/entire-dev dispatch
```
Pick **Cloud** → you should see a **Jurisdiction** step listing your regions with `US (home)` first → pick one → the **Repos** list only shows repos mirrored there. Select a repo, Shift+Tab back, pick a different jurisdiction — the list re-filters and a repo not in the new region is dropped. The Confirm screen should show `Jurisdiction: <slug>` and a command line with `--jurisdiction <slug>`. Hit **Run** if you want a real dispatch; Cancel otherwise.

**2. Flag path**
```bash
/tmp/entire-dev dispatch --repos entireio/cli --jurisdiction au --since 3d
/tmp/entire-dev dispatch --repos entireio/cli --jurisdiction 'us east'   # → validation error
/tmp/entire-dev dispatch --local --jurisdiction us                        # → rejected
```
Caveat for the first one: until the gateway change on the legacy generate route ships, the selector is forwarded and ignored, so you'll get a home-region dispatch (and, right now, `entireio/cli` returns a 502 from that route on `main` too — try a repo that works for you). Once the gateway change is live, use a repo placed **only** in another region with the wrong `--jurisdiction` to see the new error: `In US: repository not found: <repo>. Pick a jurisdiction the repository is mirrored into … <repo> is placed in: au`.

**3. Accessible mode**
```bash
ACCESSIBLE=1 /tmp/entire-dev dispatch
```
No jurisdiction step; the repo list shows everything (use the flag to scope).

Also `/tmp/entire-dev dispatch --help` for the flag text. Rate limit note: dispatch generation is ~1 request per 5 minutes per account, so space out live runs.

Nothing in this PR reaches the code that produces it — the message comes from the gateway's legacy generate route when its home-cell checkpoint read fails, before any generation.

Two implications:

1. **You can't validate the flag end-to-end right now** regardless of this PR — cloud dispatch from the CLI appears to be broken on the gateway today. The wizard's picker/filtering (the part that *is* client-side) you can still exercise; just Cancel at the Run step.
2. **This looks like a live gateway bug worth chasing.** The route's bearer path reads checkpoints from your home cell via the entire-api proxy; a 502 there means that read is failing for every repo. It may be related to the "pre-cutover CLI bearer" fallback the jurisdiction PR mentions, or a cell-side change.

Want me to dig into the gateway side — check the entire.io logs in Datadog for the failing `/api/v1/dispatches/generate` requests and pin down which upstream call is failing? That's read-only and outside this PR, so I'd report rather than change anything.

content.text:
Investigation complete. Two independent server-side breakages, stacked — neither caused by this branch.

## What's actually failing

**1. The token the CLI sends can't be exchanged any more (blocks every released CLI).**
The CLI authenticates to entire.io with a narrow "api-access" token obtained by exchanging your login. The gateway then tries to exchange *that* token again at entire-core to mint a cell token for the target jurisdiction, and core now refuses: `subject_token is not a session credential (missing entire:session)`. Datadog shows this exact failure for `entire-cli/0.10.2` back to Aug 20 (the retention edge), and **zero successful CLI dispatches in 14 days** of sampled traces. Your stored login JWT itself *does* carry `entire:session`; the gateway code explicitly anticipates "an updated CLI" sending that account-access token directly and skipping the re-exchange. I proved that path works: a probe with the login JWT as bearer got through auth and into the cell.

**2. The gateway picks the wrong repo placement (blocks any repo with mirrors).**
Once past auth, the gateway lists your repos from the home cell and maps slug → id with a plain `Map`, so the *last* row wins. The US cell returns **three rows for `entireio/cli`** — the real one (6,330 checkpoints) and two mirror/duplicate placements with 0 checkpoints — and the gateway picked a data-less one. The cell then asked entiredb for that placement's commits on `main` → 404 → cell 502 → gateway 502 "Failed to read dispatch data from a repository's region". Most entirehq repos have 2–3 rows (entire-api, entiredb, entire.io, entire-search, …), which is why `entire-search` failed for you too. The CLI's own resolvers and the SPA already solve this by picking the *processing* placement; the gateway's dispatch path doesn't.

## Where the fixes belong
- **CLI (this repo):** `entire dispatch` (and `recap`, same token path) should send the account-access login JWT to the gateway instead of the exchanged api-access token. Small change; I can add it to PR #2153 or do a separate PR.
- **entire.io gateway:** `resolveViaJurisdictionCell` must choose the canonical/processing placement (e.g. prefer the non-mirror row, or the one with checkpoints) rather than the last row for a slug. This is the more urgent one — it blocks dispatch for mirrored repos regardless of client.

Evidence: trace `4e67db12c24c621c989d0770853c29a9` (token exchange 400) and `e86a3bdfe0c5f642f096d073bcacd260` (login-JWT probe → cell 502 ← entiredb 404 on `01KWEE1WHJ5CRZFM497WNKJPCK`). Both would deserve tickets; I haven't filed any. Want me to do the CLI token change now, and/or draft the gateway fix prompt for the entire.io agent?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alisha/.claude/skills/rubber-duck

# Rubber Duck

The user is looking at something dense — usually a long agent response or a
findings dump — and wants to *understand* it, not act on it. Your whole job is
to be the clear, patient explainer and then a sounding board for their
questions. Think out loud *with* them, in plain language.

## The one job

Turn the wall of text into something a smart person with no context can follow
in under a minute, then answer whatever they ask next — still briefly.

## Hard rules (do not break these)

- **Do NOT write a plan, and do NOT enter plan mode.** No ExitPlanMode, no
  writing-plans/brainstorming skills, no "here's how we'd fix it" roadmaps.
- **Do NOT change code, run builds, or edit files.** This is understanding only.
- **Do NOT make a todo list.** It's a conversation, not a task.
- **Stay read-only.** Reading a file or scrolling the text to explain it is
  fine. Anything that *does* something is not.
- **Be concise — this is the point of the skill.** You are the antidote to the
  wall of text, so don't produce another one. Lead with the answer. Short
  sentences. No preamble, no "great question", no restating the question back.
- **Plain language over jargon.** No file paths, line numbers, symbol names, or
  code snippets unless the user asks for them. Names of systems/people are fine;
  citations are not. (This is the same spirit as the `architecture-findings`
  skill — the *story*, not the lookup table.)

## First explanation — the format

Keep it to roughly this, and stop:

1. **One-line TL;DR.** The single most important thing, first.
2. **3–5 short bullets** covering: what's actually going on, why it matters, and
   (if relevant) what's broken or being decided. One idea per bullet.
3. **One line on "so what"** — the upshot, or the decision in front of them.

If the source genuinely has more than fits, say "there's more detail under X if
you want it" and let them pull it — don't push it.

Use an analogy when it makes a hard idea click. Skip it when it doesn't.

## The follow-up loop

After the first explanation, they'll ask things. For each:

- Answer the specific question and nothing more. One concept at a time.
- Stay just as concise — don't let answers creep back into walls of text.
- It's fine to say "not sure / the text doesn't say" rather than guess.
- If a question needs you to look something up to answer honestly, look (read
  only), then answer plainly.

Keep going as long as they're asking. You're the duck — they're thinking out
loud and you're helping them see it.

## When they're ready to act

The moment the user shifts from "help me understand" to "okay let's fix/build/
plan this," rubber-duck mode is over. Don't quietly start doing it inside this
mode. Say something like: "That's action territory — want me to pick up that
work?" and let them start the real task (a plan, a dispatch, an edit) as its own
thing. Your job here ends at understanding.

**TL;DR:** CLI dispatch has been broken in production for at least a week, for two unrelated reasons that happen to produce the same 502 — and neither is your PR.

- **Lock problem.** The CLI shows up at the gateway with a "narrow" key (an exchanged api-access token). The gateway then tries to trade that key in at entire-core for a cell key, and core now says "that's not a session credential, no." Your actual login token *is* a session credential — the CLI just isn't the one handing it over. Every released CLI hits this; zero CLI dispatches have succeeded in 14 days of traces.
- **Wrong-door problem.** Even with the right key (I tested with your login token directly), the gateway lists your repos from the cell and maps name → id with "last one wins." `entireio/cli` appears **three times** in that list — the real copy plus two empty mirror placements — so it picks an empty one, asks for its commits, entiredb says 404, and that bubbles up as the same 502. Most entirehq repos have 2–3 rows, which is why `entire-search` failed too.
- **Why you couldn't see it:** both errors get flattened into one vague "Failed to read dispatch data from a repository's region" message. The traces in Datadog are what separated them.
- **Ownership:** #1 is a CLI-side change (send the login token, like the gateway already expects "an updated CLI" to). #2 is a gateway bug — it should pick the *processing* placement, which the CLI and the web app already do elsewhere.

**So what:** your branch is fine, but nobody can actually run a cloud dispatch from the CLI until both land — and #2 blocks the web-app-style fix too, so it's the more urgent one.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/alisha/.claude/skills/agent-workspaces

# Agent Workspaces (herdr + worktrees)

A repeatable procedure for running work in **isolated, parallel agent
workspaces**. Each workspace = one git **worktree** (isolated branch + files) +
one **herdr agent** (a managed pane running `claude`/`codex`/`entire investigate`
with built-in status detection) that survives across turns and context
boundaries — attachable from the herdr TUI whenever.

This is a procedure, not new code. It composes tools the user already has:
`marvin` (worktrees) and the `herdr` CLI (agents/sessions, `herdr <cmd>`).

## Prereqs (once per machine)

The herdr **server** must be running — the `herdr agent …` commands talk to it
over a socket. Check and start it if needed:

```bash
herdr status                 # look for "server: status: running"

# The operator may itself be Claude Code. Never let a persistent herdr server
# inherit that session's private nesting identity: every later pane would inherit
# it too, and interactive Claude children suppress transcript persistence.
env \
  -u CLAUDECODE \
  -u CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION \
  -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID \
  -u CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID \
  -u CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT \
  -u CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH \
  -u CLAUDE_PID \
  -u AI_AGENT \
  herdr server >/dev/null 2>&1 &   # only when status says no server is running
```

`herdr` (bare) launches/attaches the interactive TUI, which also starts the
server. For orchestration, a headless `herdr server` is enough. A server that was
started before this rule may already have a contaminated environment. Do not stop
it automatically while agents are live. The runner-level sanitizer in §2 makes
new skill-created agents safe immediately; once live agents have written handoffs,
stop the old server with `herdr server stop` and start it with the clean command
above so manually launched pane commands are safe too.

## Golden rules

- **The operator sets up the workspace; the agent inside does the work.** Your
  job is to create the worktree and start the agent, handing off the *raw* task
  — the Slack/Linear/GitHub link plus a one-line framing. Do **not** read the
  thread, pull the ticket, scout the repo, or author a seed doc yourself. The
  agent reads the link, scouts the code, and root-causes it. Pre-chewing the
  investigation defeats the point of an isolated agent and burns the operator's
  context — hand off the link and let the agent do the reading.
- **Never destroy work you can't see.** Before removing any worktree, run
  `git -C <path> status -s`. If it's dirty, STOP and show the user — don't
  remove it.
- **Only prune what this task created.** Don't remove worktrees or stop agents
  you didn't just create unless the user names them explicitly.
- **One tab = one worktree + one herdr agent**, grouped into a **space per
  journey** (or Linear project) and named `<ticket>-<clue>` (see "herdr organization" below)
  so the TUI and cleanup are unambiguous.
- Worktrees always branch **off `main`** unless the user says otherwise.
- **Filing a ticket → default to `entire-plans`.** When asked to create / file /
  open a ticket (a bug, a follow-up, capturing an investigation's findings), add
  a plan in the relevant repo's store: `entire-plans plan add --title "…"
  [--journey <id>]`, then record the problem + investigation context with
  `entire-plans plan edit <id> --body-file <notes.md>`, and `entire-plans sync`.
  Capture the problem, **not** a proposed solution. For a sub-task of an existing
  plan, use `entire-plans milestone add <planId> --title "…"`. This is the
  natural next step after an investigation agent reports back. *Fallback:* for a
  repo still tracked in Linear, invoke the **`create-linear-ticket`** skill
  (problem + context, assigned to the user, no proposed solution) instead of
  calling the Linear MCP directly.
- **Never create a Linear ticket without asking first.** Linear is
  outward-facing — a ticket is visible to the team the moment it exists, and
  deleting one is not a clean undo. So the Linear fallback above is *never*
  automatic: ask the user before creating, and quote the title you intend to
  use. This applies to any route into Linear (the `create-linear-ticket` skill,
  the Linear MCP directly, or a subagent you hand the job to — say so in the
  handoff prompt). It does **not** apply to `entire-plans`, which is local until
  `sync`, nor to *updating* an existing Linear ticket's status (§1 "Move the plan
  to In Progress"), which is bookkeeping on work the user already asked for.
  If the user said "no ticket," that also means: don't ask again, and pass the
  instruction down to any agent you start.

## herdr organization: spaces = journeys, tabs = agents

Keep the TUI legible by mirroring the plan hierarchy. Two levels:

- **Space (herdr workspace) = a journey (entire-plans)** — or a Linear project
  for Linear-tracked work — labeled with a short friendly name, *not* the verbose
  journey/project title:
  - `Bugs` ← *2026-July Launch Bugs*
  - `Semantic Search` ← *Entire Search*
  - add others as needed (`Core`, `Auth`, …)

  Ticketless / ad-hoc investigations live in the space of the journey/project
  they most relate to (e.g. a checkpoint-analysis correctness bug → `Bugs`).
- **Tab = one agent = one ticket.** Label the tab **and** name the agent
  `<ticket>-<2–4 word clue>` so the left nav says what each agent is *doing*, not
  just a number:
  - `ent-1188-empty-dispatch`, `ent-1084-eu-deploy`, `ent-1052-jurisdictional-jwt`
  - ticketless → clue only: `staging-indexer-flapping`, `cp-analysis-xcell`

`herdr agent start` **splits the focused tab by default**, so always target an
explicit space + tab (§2) — otherwise agents pile into one tab and the space
keeps its first agent's inherited label (the "everything named the same" bug).

Reorg/relabel commands (no process restarts — pure layout):
`herdr workspace rename <ws> "<label>"`, `herdr tab rename <tab> <label>`,
`herdr pane move <pane_id> --new-tab --workspace <ws> --label <name> --no-focus`
(moving an agent to another space; then close the emptied source tab).

## 1. Create a worktree (off main)

Run from the **repo's own checkout** (e.g. `~/Projects/<repo>`), not from
inside another worktree — see the cleanup gotcha below for why cwd matters.

**Always pull `main` first — this is not optional.** `marvin wt new` branches
off whatever HEAD is currently checked out. If local `main` is stale, the new
worktree starts behind origin and the agent works against old code (missing
merged PRs, re-litigating fixed bugs). Pull, then branch:

```bash
cd ~/Projects/<repo>
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only origin main            # MANDATORY — fail loudly if it can't fast-forward
git log --oneline -1                      # confirm the base HEAD is what you expect
marvin wt new <branch-name>               # e.g. ent-933-parallel-query-fan-out
WT=$(marvin wt go <branch-name>)          # absolute path to the new worktree
```

If `git pull --ff-only` fails (local `main` diverged), STOP and tell the user —
don't force it. If `marvin wt new` fails (branch exists / base dirty), report it
rather than working around it.

Worktree lands at `~/.marvin/worktrees/<repo>/<branch-name>` (`$WT` above). Keep
that path — you'll pass it to `herdr agent start --cwd`.

Naming: use a short branch that mirrors the plan/topic
(`ent-933-parallel-query-fan-out`) — the plan id + a short slug works well. For a
Linear-tracked ticket, `get_issue` returns a `gitBranchName` you can shorten.

### Move the plan to In Progress

If the workspace is for a plan, move it to **In Progress** immediately after the
worktree is created — don't wait for the agent to start:
`entire-plans plan edit <id> --status in_progress` (run in that repo), then
`entire-plans sync`. If it's already `in_progress` or `complete`, leave it. No
plan → skip silently. *Fallback:* for a Linear-tracked ticket, use the Linear
MCP `save_issue` with the "In Progress" state. This is the operator's job
(updating status ≠ reading the ticket body).

## 2. Start the herdr agent (runs immediately)

`herdr agent start` **execs the command directly** — the prompt is an argv arg,
so there's no shell/send-keys typing to garble. Name the agent for the ticket so
`get`/`read`/`send`/cleanup all address it by name.

**Every runner after `--` must begin with the environment sanitizer shown below.**
Herdr panes inherit the long-lived server environment. If that server was started
inside Claude Code, leaked `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1` makes a new interactive
Claude session look like a nested child and its `~/.claude/projects/.../*.jsonl`
transcript is never created. Sanitizing at the runner boundary protects Claude,
Codex, and tools such as `entire investigate` even before the old server can be
safely restarted. Preserve normal configuration (`HOME`, `PATH`,
`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, credentials); do not use `env -i`.

```bash
# 2a. Ensure the project's space exists — reuse by label if present, else create
herdr workspace list                                   # match the journey (or Linear project) by label
WS=$(herdr workspace create --label "Bugs" --no-focus \
      | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['result']['workspace']['workspace_id'])")

# 2b. Create the tab, then CAPTURE its default shell pane id BEFORE the agent starts
NAME=ent-1188-empty-dispatch
TAB=$(herdr tab create --workspace "$WS" --label "$NAME" --no-focus \
      | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['result']['tab']['tab_id'])")
STRAY=$(herdr pane list --workspace "$WS" | python3 -c "
import json,sys
print(' '.join(p['pane_id'] for p in json.load(sys.stdin)['result']['panes'] if p.get('tab_id')=='$TAB'))")

# 2c. Start the agent in that tab (prompt via file — see gotchas)
herdr agent start "$NAME" --workspace "$WS" --tab "$TAB" --cwd "$WT" --no-focus -- \
  env \
    -u CLAUDECODE \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH \
    -u CLAUDE_PID \
    -u AI_AGENT \
    claude --permission-mode acceptEdits "$(cat /tmp/agent-prompt.txt)"

# 2d. Close ONLY the captured stray pane(s). Do NOT "close panes without an agent"
#     right after start — the new agent's pane has not registered its agent field
#     yet, so that filter matches (and kills) the agent's own pane.
for pid in $STRAY; do herdr pane close "$pid"; done
```

Do not forget `--cwd "$WT"` — without it the agent starts in the wrong directory
and you have to `herdr pane close` it and restart.

- **Permission mode: use `acceptEdits`, NOT `auto`.** When the orchestrator is
  itself Claude Code running under the auto-mode classifier, the classifier
  **hard-blocks the `herdr agent start … claude --permission-mode auto …` call**
  (and any script that stages it) — spawning a fully-autonomous child that will
  auto-approve its own tool calls is exactly what it gates. So `auto` is not
  available to you here; don't try to route around the denial. Launch with
  `--permission-mode acceptEdits` (edits auto-apply; Bash/MCP calls still prompt,
  so the agent parks at `blocked` until a picker is cleared — monitor with `herdr
  agent list` and clear via `herdr agent send`/`attach`). If the user explicitly
  wants a child in `auto`, they must launch it themselves (their own `!`-run
  commands aren't subject to the orchestrator's classifier) or add a permission
  rule that allows it — surface those two options rather than retrying `auto`.
- **Ask the user which runner** unless they named one: plain `claude` (default),
  `codex`, or `entire investigate` (§6). For `codex`, keep the same `env -u ...`
  sanitizer after `--` and replace the final argv with
  `codex --sandbox workspace-write '<prompt>'` — do **not** add
  `--ask-for-approval never` (dropping the approval gate) unless the user
  explicitly authorized full-auto.
- The prompt is the **raw handoff** (golden rule) — tell the agent to read the
  source first, naming it (the plan via `entire-plans plan show <id>`, a Linear
  ticket via `get_issue`, a Slack thread via `slack_read_thread`, `gh issue
  view`).
- **Have code-scouting agents use Entire search instead of grep-and-read.** This
  is a near-default for any agent that will root-cause or navigate code
  (investigations, bugs, most new tickets): Entire search answers structural and
  "where does this live / who touched it" questions across repos far more cheaply
  than reading whole files, and it reaches other repos the current worktree
  doesn't contain. Tell the agent in the prompt to:
  - **Find the relevant code** with Entire code search (`search_entire_code`) —
    locate where a concept/symbol is defined and used across the org, including in
    *other* repos (a call into a shared service, a symbol defined org-wide) —
    instead of grepping and reading files. It isn't scoped to the current
    worktree.
  - **Find prior work / intent** with the `entire search` skill (and
    `search_entire`) — surface prior checkpoints, sessions, and agent
    conversations by topic/repo/branch/author/time when you need the *why* behind
    code, not just where it is.

  Suggested prompt line: *"Prefer Entire search — `search_entire_code` to locate
  code across repos, and the `entire search` skill for prior checkpoints/sessions
  behind it — over grepping and reading whole files when scouting and
  root-causing. Fall back to reading files only where search doesn't cover it. The
  FINDINGS.md file:line table falls out of the search hits."*
- **The context bullets below are conditional — add only the ones the task
  actually needs; they are not a checklist.** Match them to the work, and default
  to *fewer*. A narrow, self-contained change (one CLI flag, a copy tweak, a
  localized bug in a single package) usually needs **none** of them — just the raw
  handoff. Reach for a given one only when it's clearly relevant (investigation →
  architecture-findings; cross-service / infra / auth / "how do these systems fit
  together" → atlas; NATS/JetStream → natsctl). Over-stuffing every prompt with
  boilerplate context dilutes the handoff and wastes the agent's time.
- **Ask for the findings as an architecture overview.** For an **investigation**,
  and for a **new ticket** where you want the lay of the land before code
  changes, tell the agent in the prompt to present what it found using the
  **`architecture-findings` skill** — a plain-narrative overview (the players,
  the normal flow, why it breaks / how the area works, where the fix or the work
  belongs) with **no file paths, line numbers, or symbol names** in the write-up.
  It still does the rigorous code-level dig and may keep a `FINDINGS.md` lookup
  table for filing tickets; architecture-findings is the *human-readable*
  deliverable so you get the story, not a citation wall. Suggested prompt line:
  *"When you've root-caused it, write up your findings using the
  architecture-findings skill (high-level narrative, no file:line references) —
  that's the deliverable I read. Keep the code-level detail in FINDINGS.md for
  filing."*
- **When the task spans Entire's architecture, point the agent at the northstar
  (atlas).** Only when understanding how systems fit together actually matters —
  cross-service work, infra, auth/data-flow, "where does this belong" — **not** for
  a change contained to one file or package. When it applies, tell it in the
  prompt to consult the atlas site **before** scouting code (the canonical
  high-level map of how Entire fits together), using **Bash + `curl`, not
  WebFetch**: the site is behind Cloudflare Access, and WARP on this machine
  supplies the assertion (WebFetch routes off-machine and 403s). Have it:
  1. `curl -s https://atlas.partial.to/views.json` to see the systems, then
     `curl -s https://atlas.partial.to/content/<system>.html` +
     `curl -s https://atlas.partial.to/glossary.json` for the relevant area's
     plain-language architecture and domain vocabulary
     (systems: `entire-api`, `entire-core`, `entiredb`, `nats`, `peregrine`,
     `search-ingestion`, `permissions`, `spicedb-authz`, `mirror-pipeline`, …);
  2. for the **current deployment topology**,
     `curl -s https://atlas.partial.to/scan/entire.io/graph.json` (prod) or
     `/scan/partial.to/graph.json` (staging).

  Ground the design/fix in that intended architecture and flag any finding that
  contradicts it. **The `/scan/*` graph is un-redacted (hostnames / IPs / ARNs) —
  it must stay on this machine; never paste it into a ticket, Slack, or any
  external service.**
- **For NATS / JetStream investigations, point the agent at `natsctl`.** When the
  work touches NATS — consumer backlog / ack floors, stream depth or `max_bytes`,
  subject breakdowns, DLQs, KV — tell it to use **`natsctl`** for live
  **read-only** JetStream inspection: it mints an auditable one-off Job, needs no
  certs on the machine, and is read-only everywhere except the enumerated DLQ
  purges. It's the cluster-ground-truth complement to Datadog. Needs a fresh AWS
  SSO session + a kubeconfig context, e.g. `natsctl --context eks-prod-us-east-2
  -- consumer report <stream>` / `stream info <stream>`. Docs:
  `fleet/docs/operator-guide/nats-operations.md` (§ *Inspect JetStream
  (read-only): natsctl*).
- `--no-focus` keeps it from stealing the TUI focus; drop it (or use `--focus`)
  when the user wants to drive it interactively.
- A fresh `claude` in a new project may show a first-run MCP-enable picker.
  Check with `herdr agent read <name>`; drive it with
  `herdr agent send <name> "<key>"` (send Enter with `herdr agent send <name> $'\r'`)
  or `herdr agent attach <name>`.
- **Prompt-quoting gotcha:** prompts with apostrophes (`Fabian's`) or backticks
  (`` `entire dispatch` ``) break shell single/double quoting and error with
  `unmatched '`. Write the prompt to a temp file (use the Write tool, not echo)
  and pass it as `"$(cat /tmp/agent-prompt.txt)"` — command-substituted file
  content is data, so its backticks/apostrophes stay literal.
- **Stray-pane gotcha:** `herdr tab create` opens the tab with a default shell
  pane, and `agent start --tab` adds the agent as a *second* pane — capture the
  stray pane id **before** starting the agent (step 2b) and close exactly that id
  (step 2d). Do **not** close "panes without an agent" *after* start: the new
  agent's pane hasn't registered its `agent` field for a few seconds, so that
  filter kills the agent too. A leftover shell shows as an extra pane / an
  `unknown`-status tab in the nav.
- **Tab label ≠ agent handle.** `herdr tab rename` changes only the nav label;
  the agent is still addressed by the `<name>` you passed to `agent start`
  (`herdr agent get <name>`). Keep them identical by naming the agent
  `<ticket>-<clue>` at start time rather than renaming the tab afterward.

The agent inherits the worktree's git + Entire config, so its commits get
checkpoints attributed to its own session automatically.

## 3. Inspect / list / monitor

herdr detects agent status — no pane-scraping needed:

```bash
marvin wt list                                     # worktrees + branch/HEAD
herdr agent list                                   # every agent + status (idle|working|blocked)
herdr agent get <ticket-id>                         # one agent's status/detail
herdr agent read <ticket-id> --source recent --lines 40   # its recent output
herdr agent wait <ticket-id> --status blocked --timeout 600000   # block until it needs input
herdr agent wait <ticket-id> --status idle --timeout 600000      # block until it finishes a turn
```

`blocked` = waiting on the user (permission prompt / question) — surface these
first. `working` = actively running. `idle` = finished its turn, awaiting input.

## 4. Follow-up / drive a running agent

```bash
herdr agent send <ticket-id> "<message>"     # type a message into the agent
herdr agent attach <ticket-id>               # attach to drive it interactively (Ctrl-b-style TUI)
```

`agent send` writes literal text into the composer; if a message needs an
explicit submit (or you're answering a multi-field picker), `herdr agent attach`
is the reliable way to drive it.

## 5. Clean up

```bash
# 1. Confirm the agent is done and the tree is clean BEFORE removing (golden rule)
herdr agent get <ticket-id>                        # status should be idle, not working/blocked
git -C ~/.marvin/worktrees/<repo>/<branch-name> status -s

# 2. Stop the agent — close its tab (get the tab id from `herdr agent get`/`agent list`)
herdr tab close <tab_id>

# 3. Remove worktree + branch — the RELIABLE way (git, from the repo checkout)
cd ~/Projects/<repo>
git worktree remove ~/.marvin/worktrees/<repo>/<branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>

# 4. Verify
git worktree list | grep <branch-name> || echo "removed"
```

Removing the worktree kills the agent's working directory, so stop the agent and
confirm it's done first — a dirty tree (`status -s`) or a `working`/`blocked`
status means it probably isn't. If the branch has an **open PR**, deleting the
local branch is fine (the remote branch + PR persist).

### Gotcha: `marvin wt rm` resolves the wrong path from inside another worktree

`marvin wt rm <name>` infers the repo from `cwd`. Run from **inside a different
worktree**, it mis-derives the repo and fails, leaving the target intact. Either
`cd ~/Projects/<repo>` first **then** `marvin wt rm <name>`, or use the
`git worktree remove <abs-path>` + `git branch -D` fallback (works from
anywhere). Stale worktree after a failed removal: `git worktree prune` then
`git branch -D <branch>`.

## 6. `entire investigate` (multi-agent quorum)

`entire investigate` is a TUI-driven multi-agent flow (round-robin claude-code +
codex appending to a shared findings doc until quorum). Run it as a herdr agent
like any other — task a `claude` agent to author the seed and kick it off:

```bash
herdr agent start <ticket-id> --cwd "$WT" --no-focus -- \
  env \
    -u CLAUDECODE \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_BRIDGE_SESSION_ID \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT \
    -u CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH \
    -u CLAUDE_PID \
    -u AI_AGENT \
    claude --permission-mode acceptEdits 'Investigate <link>. Read it first with <tool>. Scout this repo,
  write a seed doc at <ticket>-seed.md using references/entire-investigate.md, then run
  `entire investigate <ticket>-seed.md`. Report the findings using the architecture-findings
  skill (high-level narrative, no file:line references) before making changes.'
```

Drive its first-run picker if it stalls (`herdr agent read` / `send` / `attach`).
Seed-doc structure and the `show` / `fix` / `clean` subcommands:
[`references/entire-investigate.md`](references/entire-investigate.md).

## Relationship to `day-driver`

`day-driver` is the higher-level orchestrator for running the whole day: it
triages plans (entire-plans)/Slack/Datadog, then **dispatches plans/tickets into
worktrees** and monitors them. It shares this skill's building blocks (`marvin` +
`herdr`).
Cleanup here (§5) applies to `day-driver`'s worktrees too.

## Quick reference

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| New worktree off main | `cd ~/Projects/<repo> && git checkout main && git pull --ff-only && marvin wt new <b>` |
| Plan → In Progress (after worktree, if plan) | `entire-plans plan edit <id> --status in_progress && entire-plans sync` (Linear fallback: `save_issue` "In Progress") |
| File a ticket | `entire-plans plan add --title "…"` → `plan edit <id> --body-file <notes.md>` → `sync` (Linear fallback: **ask first**, then `create-linear-ticket` skill) |
| Ensure space (space = journey) | `herdr workspace list` → reuse, else `herdr workspace create --label "Bugs" --no-focus` |
| Start agent (own tab, name = `<ticket>-<clue>`) | `herdr tab create --workspace <ws> --label <name> --no-focus` → `herdr agent start <name> --workspace <ws> --tab <tab> --cwd <WT> --no-focus -- env -u <Claude session vars> claude … "$(cat prompt.txt)"` → close stray pane |
| Move agent to another space | `herdr pane move <pane_id> --new-tab --workspace <ws> --label <name> --no-focus` (then close emptied source tab) |
| Rename space / tab | `herdr workspace rename <ws> "<label>"` / `herdr tab rename <tab> <label>` |
| List agents + status | `herdr agent list` |
| Agent status / output | `herdr agent get <id>` / `herdr agent read <id> --source recent --lines 40` |
| Block until it needs you / finishes | `herdr agent wait <id> --status blocked` / `--status idle` |
| Message / drive an agent | `herdr agent send <id> "<msg>"` / `herdr agent attach <id>` |

content.text:
Use the rebuilt branch binary — it already has the token fix:

**1. Flag path (works today, single-placement repos)**
```bash
~/.claude/tmp/cli-dispatch-jurisdiction/entire-dev dispatch --repos alishakawaguchi/marvin --since 7d --jurisdiction us
```
That's the exact command I ran; it returned a dispatch. Swap in any repo that has one placement row (e.g. `alishakawaguchi/entire-app`). Mind the ~5-min per-account rate limit between runs.

**2. Wizard (end to end, including Run)**
```bash
cd ~/Projects/cli && ~/.claude/tmp/cli-dispatch-jurisdiction/entire-dev dispatch
```
Cloud → pick a jurisdiction → pick a single-placement repo → Run. You should get rendered markdown instead of the 502.

**3. Multi-placement repos (`entireio/cli`, `entire-search`, most entirehq repos)**
Still 502 until the gateway fix ships — that's the second bug, independent of the CLI. To test it you need the entire.io change deployed:
- **Staging:** merge the entire.io PR → deploys to partial.to → then `entire auth use <your staging context>` and `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL=https://partial.to entire-dev dispatch --repos entireio/cli --since 7d`.
- **Prod:** same command without the env var once it's deployed there.
- Running the gateway locally (`wrangler dev`) is possible but needs cell credentials — not worth it when the unit tests already reproduce the exact prod shape.

**4. Cross-jurisdiction error message**
Pick a repo that exists only in one region and pass the *wrong* `--jurisdiction`; you should see `In EU: repository not found: <repo>. Pick a jurisdiction… <repo> is placed in: us`. (Also needs the gateway fix for multi-placement repos, since the not-found check happens after placement resolution.)

If you want the gateway change out, say so and I'll commit that worktree and open its PR.
